**Score:** 81
**Body:** Not talking about a twist for the sake of a twist, more like the kind of ending where you immediately want to rewatch the whole thing because you know you'll see it differently now that you have the full picture.

Open to any genre, just want that specific feeling of the movie folding back on itself in a way that actually earns it

Memento
2. The Usual Suspects
3. The Prestige
4. Psycho, Shutter Island, Sixth Sense, Red Notice, Fight Club, Saw.

**Score:** 64

all the movies ive watched have left me with medium emotions ("oh wow!" "aww..") and let me fucking tell you - this movie was **GENUINELY CINEMA.. I WAS IN SHOCK (and not at the graphics!)**

**I CANNOT RECOMMEND THIS ENOUGH, 10/10 MOVIE - ON NETFLIX.**

## 4. Want a detective movie

**Score:** 47
**Body:** I'm looking for a detective thriller with a lonely, emotionally distant protagonist who is deeply consumed by solving a mystery. I prefer a dark, moody atmosphere with strong noir vibes, slow-burn pacing, psychological tension, and a sense of isolation. The story should focus on investigation, suspense, and character depth rather than nonstop action. I enjoy films with haunting cinematography, memorable soundtracks, morally complex characters, and mysteries that keep me thinking long after the ending. Serial killer investigations, missing person cases, or conspiracies are all welcome, as long as the film maintains a serious, immersive tone. I'd appreciate recommendations that are highly rated, underrated, or international, and please avoid lighthearted detective stories or movies that rely mainly on action or comedy.

## 2. Tom Holland is this generations Michael J. Fox After BND and The Odyssey hold the top 2 spots at the box office simultaneously

**Score:** 1174
**Body:** In 2021 on The Hot Ones Tom Holland said he based his portrayal of Peter Parker on Back to the Future, that he wanted to be this generation’s Marty McFly. Well holy manifestation Batman, Tom Holland just did something that Michael J. Fox did 40 years ago. That is hold the number 1 and number 2 spots at the box office simultaneously with Spider Man Brand New Day and The Odyssey.

In the summer of 1985 Back to the Future held the top spot at the box office week after week after week. Late in August Teen Wolf was released, and although it did not knock BTTF off the top spot, it was #2 at the box office its opening weekend.

Some will say Michael J. Fox is still the undisputed champion as he was clearly the leading man of both films whereas Tom played a very prominent role in the Odyssey, but he was not #1 on the call sheet. But for Tom, who shares the #1 and #2 spot with his wife Zendaya and his friend John Bernthal, it is an absolutely astonishing accomplishment that he has seemingly just willed into existence.

3. There has been no Michael J Fox since Michael J Fox. He's such a uniqe actor. BttF would never have worked as well without his timing and energy.
4. OR.... hear me out. Tom Holland is Tom Holland & MJ Fox is MJ Fox... they are their own people in their own time. 🤯
5. If you remove MJF charm and good acting, sure, they’re comparable.
6. Tom Holland doesn't hold a candle to Michael. They are not in the same league anything.
7. I like Tom Holland but Michael j Fox is a perfect blend of cool/nerdy that I think doesn’t align with Tom holland. I’d say MJF is closer to Andrew Garfield 
8. Tbf, holland is a side character in the odyssey. And I think he’s horribly miscast
9. I’m not as convinced Tom Holland has any acting power and draw outside Spider-Man.

Spider-man has really been his only role. Sure the Odyssey was a hit but you could have replaced Tom Holland with anyway and it would still have been a great movie and a hit because it was a Nolan film. None of Tom’s other movies went anywhere.

Also, few people anywhere are talking about Tom in the Odyssey being an amazing performance. It was just ok.

Tom Holland is Spider-man, and I think he will always be seen as Spider-Man and he will struggle to get out of that shadow. 

Likely everything else he does outside Spider-Man, he won’t be able to carry it unless another big name is attached. 

I could be proven wrong but the evidence kinda speaks to it at the moment.
  - I'd argue Tom could've been replaced by many people in the Odyssey and it would've improved the movie. 

## 3. Why was Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri so polarizing?

**Score:** 976

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Don't know what others may know about the inspiration behind this movie, but outside my home city near the smaller town of Vidor were billboards along interstate 10 reading:

IN VIDOR

YOU CAN

GET AWAY

WITH MURDER

followed by other billboards as you got into town describing the death of Kathy Page, strangled and basically ignored as a case for cops. Her husband Steve Page was initially a prime suspect, but claims of not enough evidence has left it unsolved; he currently lives in Houston.

Many, including of course her father, have demanded justice through the charge and conviction of Steve Page. But there's never been enough evidence. They claim it's because of the lackadasical efforts of the Vidor PD. It remains "unsolved", and their own police department wants to just close the case at this point....
  - Oh man, I remember when we moved to Orange from the Midwest when I was a kid. Driving through Vidor and seeing those billboards for the first time is a core memory for me. “Where the hell are they moving me to?” crossed my mind. 
2. My first watch I hated it because I felt Sam Rockwell's character's redemption arc was unearned compared to the harm he did in the preceding scenes. I found it a bleak, nasty piece of work.

But I couldn't stop thinking about it and I wanted to know why I had a visceral reacton to it,  so I saw it again.  Now I love it. 
  - It's not full redemption. It's the hope of redemption. He's taking a substantial step towards changing for the better. The promise of doing better to make up for his past.
  - I see it less as a redemption arc and more as the first step. Even the biggest, worst asshole you know has the capacity to change
  - I get it. Growing up in a rural town, this was too real... I wish more people had the redemption arc sam has in real life. Instead I'm surrounded by poor people telling me how great everything is and only using their effort to own the "librards."
3. Some people wanted a fourth billboard
4. Not polarizing at all. This one is nearly universally loved and rightly so.
  - I love Peter Dinklage in this. Setting fire to the police station in the evenin time just kills me. 
5. For the people saying “tough watch”, I didn’t rewatch for a long time because that was my takeaway. When I did rewatch, I had forgotten how much dark humor there was.

“What?”  
“Don’t say what when she comes in calling you a dickhead!”

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Deep Thought: The People in Classic Movies Are Gone, But Their Effort Isn't

**Score:** 52
**Body:** Most people say they watch old movies because of the incredible filmmaking, the emotional storytelling, or the beautiful simplicity of a different era.

Those are all reasons I love them too.

But the biggest reason is that I honour the people.

When I watch a film from the 1950s or 1960s or any retro movies, I think about everyone on that screen. Not just the stars, but the background actors, the costume designers, the makeup artists, the lighting crew, and every person who poured a piece of themselves into creating something they believed mattered.

At the time, it was real life to them. They memorized lines, rehearsed scenes, put on carefully tailored clothes, styled their hair, laughed, cried, worried about getting everything right, and spent months creating something that would outlive the moment.

Now it's 2026.

Almost all of them are gone. Their bodies have returned to dust, yet their energy still reaches across time through the screen. I can still feel the sincerity in their performances. Their effort still exists in a strange way, even though the people themselves do not.

It reminds me how temporary our lives are.

The things that seem enormous today, our careers, our appearance, our achievements, eventually become distant memories, and then, for most people, forgotten altogether.

Yet the love, care, and effort we put into something can echo far beyond us.

It makes me wonder whether we're investing our energy in things that disappear with us, or in things that continue touching people long after we're gone.

Maybe that's the closest we ever come to creating something eternal.

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. This is a lovely perspective. I think similar thoughts. When I watch an old movie, it's a window into the era it was made: a time and place that no longer exists. The film is a message in a bottle. The people onscreen, and just offscreen, were living lives in a world that has changed so much. All of their life experience, knowledge, skill, craft, and their hopes and fears, show up in the final product.

My interest is Japanese films of the 1950s-1970s. Sometimes I can't stop thinking, "Every single person onscreen lived through WW2. Also, everyone who saw the film when it first came out." That can be an important part of understanding what the film is really about.
  - I was watching an interview with Kaneto Shindo just yesterday. 

He spoke with a simple but sincere power about living through WW2, the struggles that he and his filmmaking peers went through, before, during and after. 

He only spoke about the filmmaking side of things. But the hunger, poverty, fear and indignity of it all is there to see in his work.

I am yet to see his film “Children of Hiroshima”, his childhood home, completely obliterated. 
  - Oooh yeah I've had this perspective a lot with that 60's and early 70's period of European cinema. All my grandparents had already passed away by the time I was born and it's like a way to get a glimpse into the world when  they were around my age.
2. I absolutely agree. It's also part of the reason I like to watch the full credits of movies in theaters and just look at random names and think "Good job, y'all!"\*

It's also a lot of fun to read some really interesting and unusual names go by.

\*(Slightly less interesting nowadays with the huge blocks of credits for all the effects houses typically involved.)

I HATE that all the streamers won't let me watch credits in peace and sit with the movie for a bit after viewing, and just immediately slam me with ads for other movies. I wish there was a setting I could toggle for that on the apps.
  - Not to mention that streaming platforms have the technology to turn every name in the credits into a hyperlink to, say, IMDb or Wikipedia to learn more about them and their work.

Amazon Prime Video used to have a similar functionality when actors were on-screen, but I think they axed it.
3. This is a beautiful, poignant and respectful way of honouring the film family that has gone before. Immortalised, as you say, and offering up such rich windows into their lives, which we can only imagine.

One phrase stuck out….

“the beautiful simplicity of a different era”.

There’s an interesting gap opening up between films now and then, between the handling of complexity and presenting with simplicity. 

Filmmakers of say the early 20th century lived through unimaginable complexity, chaos and confusion. Not just two world wars but a Great Depression, huge ideological clashes, revolutions and independence struggles, rapid technological and societal change. Their lives were far from simple.

Now. This may be somewhat romantic (and it’s obviously quite a generalisation) but I find there is a remarkable capacity in say pre-1970s films to grasp and handle complexity with a deft, delicate and distilling touch. And also extend a respect for their audience to sit with complexity and find their own way and meaning through it.

Compare that with today and we find a strange impulse to increase complexity on screen and yet, somehow, also leave audiences with not much to think about: Too much exposition. Tying it all up too neatly. Serving up conclusions and not leaving viewers to chew over the mystery. 

I wonder what those earlier filmmakers would make of how we handle our stories and audiences today.
4. It is my understanding. Clint Eastwood is the oldest living top billing actor. William Shatner was in some old ones as well, just not at top billing. Everyone before them is gone now.
5. This sentiment reminds me of Jean Smart’s monologue to Brad Pitt’s character in Babylon about how he will live on in movies long after he is dead, a type of immortality: “Your time today is through, but you’ll spend eternity with angels and ghosts.” 

## 2. What Have You Been Watching? (Week of (August 02, 2026)

**Score:** 8
**Body:**  Please don't downvote opinions. Only downvote comments that don't contribute anything. Check out the [WHYBW archives](https://www.reddit.com/r/TrueFilm/wiki/index#wiki_what_have_you_been_watching.3F).

### Top 3 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. **The Devil Wears Prada 2 (2026, David Frankel)**

Fun watch and absolutely love Meryl Streep and Anne Hathaway. Runtime was far too long though, should’ve been closer to 1 hour not 2 hours. **5.5/10**

**The Odyssey (2026, Christopher Nolan)**

I was lucky enough to watch this on 70mm IMAX and it was an incredible experience!!! Visually stunning, a true epic that was engaging all throughout. Casting was great, I thought Matt Damon put on a good performance (solid not impressive though). Thoroughly enjoyed it! **9.5/10**
2. **Autumn Sonata (1978, dir. Ingmar Bergman)**

Phenomenal picture. Bergman's writing is cutting and painful, and Liv Ullman and Ingrid Bergman do the material justice and then some. I didn't know anything about the film going in, so I appreciated the escalation. It starts out as a decently relaxing foray into a beautiful fjord cottage, but carefully grows into something a lot less charming and a lot more emotionally difficult. The dialogue is natural, even when the writing gets outwardly philosophical, and Bergman's hand is balanced, never fully denouncing either character for their sins. It's a very visceral film, incisive in the way that a truly great poem or symphony is. I loved it when I watched it, and I think I'll grow to love it even more as time goes on.

**Tinsman Road (2025, dir. Robbie Banfitch)**

Derivative of other found footage movies like The Blair Witch Project and Lake Mungo, but Tinsman Road is distinguished by how it uses its medium. The camera quality is crusty and subpar, and the protagonist, Robbie Lyle (not to be confused with Robbie Banfitch, who plays the character and directs), can't frame a shot to save his life - literally. This, along with plenty of asides exploring the quaint and sometimes creepy setting of rural New Jersey, lends the film an air of authenticity. The atmosphere of the woods is omnipresent regardless of whether or not someone is shooting it. Robbie is just someone out of his element getting caught up in something unsettling and beyond his capacity to understand. The story is a little repetitive and less interesting than the filmmaking, but it's carried surprisingly well by actors who are all but playing themselves. Leslie Banfitch is the real star of the film. What a cold mother, but who can blame her when she's lost so much?

**Forelock (2025, dir. Caleb Alexander Smith)**

Fun crime comedy. The premise is novel and approaches the classic story of a middle American hoping to find success as an actor in LA from a really neat angle with a lot of room to move around the city geographically and socially. The story is convoluted and full of twists, turns, conspiracies, and danger, but the direction is light enough to keep the movie from feeling too unrealistic or contrived. Smith plays off of a scuzzy drug dealer really well, emulating buddy comedies from yesteryear we don't see very much anymore. The comedy is solid, and the character development is good too. At the end of the day, Forelock is a story about finding yourself and reaching your ambition when the universe only throws you curveballs, and when it tries to be heartfelt and serious it succeeds. It kind of has it all. I hope Forelock gets a wider release one day, because I think people will get a kick out of it and Smith has the capacity to go far in the movies.

**Prometheus (2012, dir. Ridley Scott)**

There's a bookstore in town where you can fill a bag with books and buy all of them for five dollars. The books are all one or two dollars apiece, so if you play your cards right you can save ten dollars on a bunch of literature. I really like going down to the store and rifling through the sci-fi/fantasy section for any book that might be interesting. What winds up here is mostly idea-driven pulpy sci-fi from the 1980s that relies on violence, sex, and mood more than sound character and plot. These aren't books that I'd ordinarily buy online or from larger retailers, but at the little bookstores they're basically free, and you never know. I've developed an affinity for these books and the schlockier side of sci-fi, and Prometheus fit nicely into that niche. This is problematic, because Scott clearly wants the viewer to take Prometheus seriously as some provocative treatise on humanity and our origins. I don't think the writing is there, though. The characters are simply drawn, and the philosophical and cultural side of the film is underbaked. You can't expect me to take seriously the idea that some company would invest trillions of dollars into a space mission because some archaeologists found some drawings that they foolishly believe mean that ancient aliens gave them technology. Once you get past some iffy stuff in the set-up, I think the horror sequences are effective and the film moves at a decent pace, slowly showing how everything falls apart before some action in the third act that ties everything together. At that point, the film's tenuous grasp on me slackened as I was forcibly reminded that this is an Alien prequel. Fuck that. The space jockey in Alien is way more interesting as some weird mystery than as a demigod carting some of his own bioweapons after Guy Ritchie tried to make himself immortal. I don't know what Scott was thinking there. But clearly he did something right because Prometheus was largely entertaining. If it were made as a stand-alone sci-fi horror movie in 1986, it would be a certified cult classic.

**A Little Princess (1917, dir. Marshall Neilan)**

This movie is notable for having 25-year-old Mary Pickford play a ten-year-old girl. I thought she was stretching it as a teenager in 1916, but someone wanted to milk her for all her youthfulness apparently. The effect is actually done pretty convincingly in wide shots in this movie, utilizing costuming, forced perspective, and set design to impressive degrees, but it's still really distracting. Looking past Pickford, I like parts of the story but I think it's all paced rather poorly. Pickford plays the daughter of a wealthy man doing work in India, necessitating Pickford's placement in a girls' home in London. The man dies overseas, and Pickford is kept in the home but loses her privileges and becomes a slave for the headmistress. The film is just over an hour long, but it spends much too much time on Pickford's life before her father dies. We see her making friends and enemies in the home, which never comes into play in the rest of the movie, and spend a good fifteen minutes on a well-produced but ultimately pointless retelling of Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves. I like the relationship Pickford develops with another slave girl and how Pickford learns humility and to appreciate her innocence, but this isn't given a lot of time to develop satisfyingly. Give this movie another thirty, sixty minutes and it could be a decent coming-of-age story with entertaining fantasy sequences and interesting cinematography.

**Ga-ga: Glory to the Heroes (1986, dir. Piotr Szulkin)**

When I watched this movie, I didn't realize that it was part of a series of four movies by Szulkin called the Apocalypse Tetralogy. They're connected only thematically and aesthetically, but Ga-ga was the last film and the culmination of Szulkin's cinematic style. Looking back, I think that this lack of context threw me for a loop with Ga-ga. The film initially struck me as an overwhelming pastiche of so many different sources - Kafka, Gilliam, Adams, and Stephen King by way of Richard Bachman. Even the matter-of-fact way that protagonist Scope came across this weird, incomprehensible world reminded me of how Tarkovsky depicted illusory characters in Solaris. The plot of Ga-ga operates on dreamlike logic, throwing Scope from one weird scenario into another and expecting you the viewer to put these things together. The film ultimately makes commentary on prisoners, crime, and punishment. In the future, Earth is so prosperous that humans no longer feel the need to explore space, so the government turns prisoners into astronauts who are forced to survey alien worlds. Scope lands on a planet where rulebreakers are killed in celebratory executions and literally hailed as heroes. This is the lynchpin of the alien society, and when Scope is chosen to be a hero, they try to get him to commit a crime so they'll have an excuse to execute him. The texture of the film makes it difficult to easily extract holistic interpretations, but I certainly enjoyed watching it. It's a rather funny movie and vague enough to apply to 21st century America as well as 1980s Poland.
  - 
**Golem (1980, dir. Piotr Szulkin)**

After watching Ga-ga, I was interested in going through the rest of the Apocalypse Tetralogy in the hopes that I would get some context that could help me make sense of Ga-ga. What better place to start than Golem, Szulkin's first feature? My favorite aspects of Ga-ga were its comments on free will, and Golem revels in this conversation. Golem is an adaptation of the Jewish folk tale of the golem, a man made of clay who can be brought to life in order to defend a town. In Szulkin's interpretation, the golem is a genetic experiment named Pernat, living in a post-nuclear war world where the government is looking for ways to quickly repopulate the human race. As in Ga-ga, the storytelling of Golem is haywire and difficult to follow, but I think it communicates its themes in really interesting and clear ways. Pernat doesn't know he's a golem in the beginning, and is seeded in society by the government in order to experiment with individualism. He comes to terms with his condition over the course of the film, realizing how labyrinthine his life is as the government does everything in its power to exert control over him. Szulkin asks us what liberty looks like in a society that cannot abide it, and expresses these questions in a surreal, almost incomprehensible but still potent style characterized by dilapidated cities and heavy green lighting. It's difficult to really describe how Byzantine the story of the film is. It's the kind of thing you really have to experience.

**The War of the Worlds: Next Century (1981, dir. Piotr Szulkin)**

This is my favorite of the Apocalypse Tetralogy. Szulkin adapts HG Wells' The War of the Worlds, but instead of showing battles and chaos he opts for a meditation on collaboration and colonialism. The world of Next Century has already been subjugated by (or has subjugated itself to) the Martians, believing the aliens to be far more advanced and therefore better than humans in every way. Responding to chaos we don't see, the government locks down cities and monitors its citizens, classifying some as friends of the Martians and keeping tabs on blood type, as human blood is a resource prized by the Martians. The film follows Iron Idem, a television broadcaster who, against his better judgement, is forced to anchor a propaganda program instructing the people that the Martians are good and to trust government regulations and instructions. Idem loses his composure and resists the aliens, grappling with the nebulous machine of government propaganda itself. The commentary feels as fresh now as it did forty years and half a world away. The people of Next Century are scared and confused and will confide in the most logical and consistent friend they have: mass media. This becomes their moral undoing, which Idem tries and fails to resist in ways that bring to mind Network more than traditional adaptation of the Wells novel. I strongly recommend The War of the Worlds: Next Century. It's sci-fi as its ablest and most pertinent, and well-produced to boot.

**O-Bi, O-Ba: The End of Civilization (1985, dir. Piotr Szulkin)**

O-Bi, O-Ba is as well produced as the rest of the Apocalypse Tetralogy, but I found the story a little lacking. The film is set one year after nuclear war. During the initial exchange, two thousand people were shepherded into a dome in the mountains, and now the dome is failing to hold back lethal radiation and nuclear winter and all but 875 have died. But no one is willing to accept death because they believe that a spaceship, the Ark, is coming to ferry everyone away to a better life. Protagonist Soft, who spread the Ark story in the first place to boost morale, is tasked with convincing people that the Ark is actually fiction, but he becomes enamored with the story himself. Soft lacks the complex characterization of Idem in War of the Worlds: Next Century and the sympathy of Pernat in Golem, and I didn't mind much for this film's protagonist. He seemed aimless, and the story was similarly stuck in a loop exploring different perspectives on the Ark and humanity's prognosis. Little new information is gleaned for the first hour of the film, and it feels more interested in showing off admittedly excellent production design instead of telling a coherent story. The third act picks up, invoking staggering imagery and some of Szulkin's trademark surrealism. I love how the ending isn't a copout and maintains the bleakness of the rest of the film without feeling fully like a downer. It, and O-Bi, O-Ba overall, is a pretty sound ending to my nonlinear tour of the Apocalypse Tetralogy, even if I liked other movies in the series more. Overall, it's a great tetralogy, and I'd recommend them to anyone who loves good sci-fi.

**Lurker (2025, dir. Alex Russell)**

Lurker is largely very good. The writing is mostly strong, and the performances are even better. The story taps into anxieties about parasocial relationships really well, invoking plenty of older and newer thrillers while still standing on its own. The story revolves around a gawky young man, Matthew, who's invited into the entourage of his favorite pop star, Oliver. When he realizes that he was only invited so he could do housework at Oliver's house, he decides to manipulate photoshoots and music videos to sabotage other entourage members' careers, drawing him closer to Oliver. The escalation in this film is tense and shocking, but at a certain point it reaches a plateau. I think the last forty minutes are strange and at odds with the rest of the film, introducing concepts that weren't really present beforehand and changing the tone a bit. The ending is especially strange. I don't even know what Russell was thinking with this. But whatever problems exist in the back half of Lurker don't overshadow its strengths, especially its performances. Theodore Pellerin is incredible in this film. Keep an eye out for him.

**The Battle of Algiers (1966, dir. Gillo Pontecorvo)**

Fantastic film. Not a thing about it feels dated. The way it depicts violence is so gritty and real, even if I've seen more convincing violence in other movies. It understands the human cost of war and colonialism so well and is a lot less one-sided than I was expecting, especially after I saw that this was commissioned by the nascent Algerian government. It obviously sympathizes more with the indigenous Algerians than the French colonists, but it's not afraid to show how gruesome Algerian violence against French civilians can be and characterizes characters like Colonel Mathieu in nuanced, realistic ways that don't cast them as mustache-twirling villains. The film understands that war is limiting and meaningful change will always come from a pen instead of the barrel of a gun. It's a brutal picture with excellent cinematography, editing, voiceover, and acting. I'll be damned if it isn't one of my favorite war movies now.

**Deep Red (1975, dir. Dario Argento)**

After hearing about giallo for almost a decade now, I decided to give it a try, and I didn't really like it. Argento clearly knows how to frame a shot and how to make use of color, but the performances were hokey, the story was tedious, and whatever strength the editing had was undercut by that damn Goblin score. I know people like that, but I couldn't stand it. One day I'll get around to some of Lucio Folce's movies, and hopefully I'll get the appeal of those more.
3. **The Great Escape (1963, John Sturges) — re-watch** — Still think this is probably the best of the all-star showoff movies of the 50s and 60s. Basically perfect. **10/10**

**Hercules (1997, John Musker/Ron Clements)** — I don’t have enough familiarity with the deep cuts of the Disney animated canon to say definitively that the 1997 *Hercules* is definitively their all-time worst animated feature, but I would be very surprised if it isn’t at least in competition for the title. For a while as I was watching it, I was a little confused as to why discourse around the movie tends to treat Hades being a villain as its main deviation from mythology, given that he’s really no less faithful to the source material than any other character; if anything, he might be the only character whose mythic personality is left at least very vaguely recognizable. On reflection, I think I do get why this is: in order to criticize the portrayals of characters other than Hades, you would have to first remember that there are other characters in the movie at all, which is not easy to do when, across the entire movie, no other character gets even a single memorable moment. **4/10**

**Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas (1998, Terry Gilliam)** — Loved this way more than I expected. I’ll be curious to see how it’ll play on rewatches, but for now, I basically have no complaints. **10/10**

It’s just that the wonderful comedy and musical bits which make it great are all pretty obvious immediately, and the movie’s few attempts to aim for something deeper or more complex than surface-level humour and spectacle tend to be the points where it’s at its weakest. Highly recommended. **8/10**

**Battlestar Galactica (1978, Richard A. Colla/Alan Levi)** — I have not seen either television version of *Battlestar Galactica*, but I’d heard that the original version from the ’70s is just a hodgepodge of elements lazily ripped off from other sci-fi franchises. ## 4. Crowd reaction at the end of The Odyssey

**Score:** 0
**Body:** Just saw The Odyssey this evening in IMAX 70mm and enjoyed it overall, but I was taken aback by the crowd’s applause towards the end of the film when Odysseus reveals himself and takes on the suitors.

As the film went on, I started to view Odysseus as an anti-hero of sorts. I first felt this way during the Cyclops sequence when he shot the extra arrow, prompting the Cyclops to come raging after them. There was no additional benefit from shooting that arrow and contributed to Poseidon cursing his crew later on. His maverick decision-making and deceptive nature isolates him from his crew and further leads to their downfall. 

After the Cyclops incident and battle with the Giants, his crew’s trust in him dwindles. When they get to Circe’s island, he’s forced to hunt separately while his crew is morphed into pigs by Circe. Odysseus saves them, but he should’ve been leading them to begin with. He later learns about his prophecy in the underworld and tries hard to save his crew from the worst. While passing the sirens, he feels the urge to listen to the song of the sirens while his men insert wax into their ears to stay on board. It was confusing why he felt the need to do that and it only put his men at more risk. Later on, his men get so fed up that they eat some cattle behind Oddyseus’ back on the one cursed island, which leads to their deaths in the ocean.

I think Odysseus did a great job infiltrating Troy with his men, but he had to deceive the Trojans and one of his own men (the Eliot Page character) in order to make it a success. After they opened the gates and started attacking Troy, he had to grapple with the violence that ensued after. It seemed like that really messed with his psyche, since he made some mistakes that cost the lives of his men while he was returning home. I think he felt obligated to lead while carrying the burden of survivor’s guilt after losing a number of men. He slowly began to lose credibility amongst his men as the film went on, and he was only left with himself at the end. I felt bad for Odysseus but I also felt like some of the violence could have been prevented and he was somewhat to blame.

Near the end of the film when Odysseus returns and reveals himself, I was somewhat confused when the crowd in the theater started to applaud as if he were a hero returning for vengeance. It seemed like the crowd forgot everything that had transpired for the first couple hours. Why were people rooting for more violence, as if it would make up for the mistakes that cost his men their lives earlier in the film? Of course I wanted him to reunite with his family, but it didn’t feel very heroic to me. It felt like I was watching a Vietnam War vet with PTSD come home and kill a guy his wife had been cheating on him with while he was overseas. It just felt weird hearing applause for that scene.

Did anyone else experience this in theaters? Curious to get other opinions, maybe I’m misinterpreting how it ended.

## 5. Another Nolan's Odyssey Review, but Centered on the Writing and Cinematography

**Score:** 0
**Body:** *The Odyssey* was not a bad movie. I enjoyed it. The acting was strong, most of the characters were compelling, and the production felt refreshingly physical. Rather than building the entire world out of CGI, the film used tangible sets, landscapes, and locations that gave the journey weight. The cities looked closer to modest settlements and rocky strongholds than enormous marble metropolises, which felt right for the Bronze Age. The costumes were not especially accurate, but the world itself still felt lived in.

My largest problem was not the casting or the American accents. It was the gap between how the writing described Odysseus and how he actually behaved.

Everyone repeatedly calls him cunning, conniving, and exceptionally intelligent. We hear that he devised the Trojan Horse and that he was Agamemnon's cleverest general. However, the film rarely lets us witness that intelligence for ourselves. Characters praise his mind, but the plot supplies almost no evidence to support them.

The Cyclops sequence exposes the problem most clearly. In the original story, Odysseus tells Polyphemus that his name is "Nobody," allowing the wounded Cyclops to tell the others that nobody is attacking him. He also intoxicates him with lotus-infused wine before blinding him, which helps establish the sleepy/amnesiac effects of the lotus flowers. These choices establish the defining qualities as he manipulates language, plans ahead, and understands his enemy.

The film removes that strategy. Instead of a battle of wits, the Cyclops is a nameless, lumbering beast that just attacks them when they enter his cave and then unceremoniously falls asleep. Instead of watching him improvise a brilliant escape, we watch another dangerous encounter happen around him. Removing these details strips Odysseus of the intelligence the screenplay keeps insisting that he possesses.

Much of the journey follows an "and then" structure. The men wash onto an island, encounter something terrible, flee, and arrive somewhere else to be attacked again. Events accumulate, but Odysseus is not the one leading his men so much as the narrative. 

The real problem is how little urgency Odysseus shows after Tiresias tells him that every member of his crew will die. He does not desperately fight the prophecy or push himself to find some way around it. He mostly sits there warning them in an almost bored tone that something is dangerous and that they are all going to die. They ignore him, the disaster happens, and he responds with the same weary “I told you this would not work” attitude before they move on to the next catastrophe A stronger film would have made the prophecy a source of conflict, with Odysseus fighting to outwit it only to discover his attempts were helping fulfil it. His intelligence could have become both his greatest weapon and the mechanism of his destruction. Instead, the prophecy mostly functions as advance notice for scenes the audience already knows will end badly.

The deaths also lack emotional weight because the crew remains largely anonymous. We hear fragments suggesting some of these men have families, fears, or histories, but the film rarely develops them as individuals. Their relationship with Odysseus never feels deep enough to justify the grief their deaths are meant to carry. The *Lord of the Rings* gives Legolas, Gimli, Aragorn, Boromir, and the hobbits separate loyalties, conflicts, histories, and ways of seeing the world. Odysseus's crew, by contrast, feels like a large group of exhausted comrades travelling home after a raid. We understand they are tired and that Odysseus has lost his men, but we do not feel that specific people have been lost.

The retrospective structure also weakens the story. Beginning with Telemachus and telling Odysseus's journey through recollection creates distance from the suffering that supposedly defines him. We never experience the grinding ten-year siege of Troy, never see the Greeks repeatedly fail to take the city, and never watch the frustration and brutality that produced the rage Odysseus later claims helped doom their world. Even two minutes showing the Greeks trapped on the beach, exhausted by years of failed assaults, would have given his anger a foundation.

Some of the dialogue becomes especially clunky near the end. Odysseus referring to "this age of bronze of ours" was jarring, since people living during the period would not have understood themselves as inhabitants of a historical category invented later by scholars. Similar language about the end of civilization feels equally artificial. The characters could certainly have feared the destruction of their kingdoms, gods, and customs. They would not likely have spoken with the detached historical awareness of people already reading about the Bronze Age collapse in a textbook.

The pacing also felt uneven. Some cuts were jarring, and the shaky camera work occasionally blurred action that needed clarity. Shots that called for a wide or low angle were often replaced by close-ups, and moments meant to show us what a character was seeing were reduced to shots of a face and the reaction. The lighting fared better and was a genuine strength, especially during the storm sequences.

My biggest issue, though, is Athena. In the original poem she is Odysseus's patron and long-time protector, drawn to him because his cunning mirrors her own, and the text takes care to establish why she keeps intervening on his behalf. That relationship has a history, even if most viewers have never read the poem and would not recognize her without help. The film never bothers with that groundwork. Athena simply begins appearing to Odysseus and speaking to him as though the two share some connection, with nothing shown to explain why.

Despite these problems, I still enjoyed the film. Its physical production, performances, atmosphere, and willingness to portray the ancient world as rough and human rather than impossibly grand gave it real value. It often felt like an older kind of historical epic, one where the actors were standing inside a world rather than floating in front of one.

Why doesn't Polyphemus say - look at all the men in this cave, one of them said his name was Nobody, and they stabbed me in the eye?

Why don't any of the other cyclops look around the cave?

It doesn't make any sense, unless you accept that Polyphemus is a complete idiot or the other Cyclops are blind.  Maybe this punning worked 3000 years ago. It sure as heck doesn't work visually now. Similarly Nolan has the Greeks tie grass to their armor to cloak themselves as sheep rather than tying themselves to the bellies of the sheep and having the sheep somehow carry men out of the cave as in the poem.
7. >Everyone repeatedly calls him cunning, conniving, and exceptionally intelligent. We hear that he devised the Trojan Horse and that he was Agamemnon's cleverest general. However, the film rarely lets us witness that intelligence for ourselves. Characters praise his mind, but the plot supplies almost no evidence to support them.

Sidenote: this reminds me of a cliche in film, often of female characters, who are described or positioned as one of the smartest people in a field (astrophysicist? linguist? I don't know) or even on Earth (!), but then never get to actually do or say anything with much intelligence. Did Odysseus get the "genius female character" treatment? 
8. Half of the cinematography was adequate and the other half was poor. I get it that the IMAX camera is a beast but that still shouldn't prevent Nolan from composing shots in a creative fashion. The dialogue scenes were the worst and maybe he just needed to rush through those scenes since the action scenes were going to consume much of the shooting schedule. The compositions certainly didn't help to distract from the poor dialogue.

It was an empty shell of a film that had a lot of potential but needed a different director to pull it off. Of the popular mainstream directors today, I actually think that Denis V. would have given us a much more compelling film that would do more than try and modernize the story a bit and deliver some interesting action/set pieces.
